item.title: A buried river was uncovered in Yonkers; 6 months later, wildlife had a 14,000 sq ft habitat
item.description: In 2012, Yonkers, New York, completed a project to uncover a section of the Saw Mill River that had been buried beneath a downtown parking lot since the 1920s. The former Larkin Plaza was turned into a three-acre public park. Within six months, the restored river supported 14,000 square feet of new aquatic habitat and several species.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: QTCinderella’s homophobic friends controversy explained: Streamer under fire over past comments
item.description: QTCinderella has responded after renewed criticism over claims that she associates with “homophobic people.” The streamer explained that she believes kindness and personal relationships can help people reconsider harmful beliefs. She also admitted that her comments from a year ago were poorly worded and said she is not friends with bigots. After more confusion online, she shared a longer explanation on her main X account.
item.dc:creator: Global Sports Desk

item.title: New Haven landfull turned into solar farm now powers about 200 homes and pays the city $72,000 a year
item.description: New Haven is transforming a decommissioned landfill into a major solar energy project, installation of 1,920 solar panels that will produce a significant amount of clean energy every year. With anticipated revenue exceeding $1.4 million over two decades, this venture supports New Haven's dedication to enhancing its renewable energy initiatives, ultimately benefitting both the environment and the local economy.

item.title: Meet Zac Waters, the 13-year-old who spent 300 hrs 3D-printing wheelchair for a 21-month-old
item.description: A 13-year-old boy from Lehi, Utah, spent about 300 hours during his summer designing, printing, testing and assembling a custom mobility chair for a 21-month-old girl. Zac Waters found MakeGood, a nonprofit that provides free 3D-printed mobility devices, and used his interest in 3D printing to build a chair tailored to the toddler’s needs.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: In 1977, a Saudi prince towed an Alaskan iceberg to Iowa; now engineers are exploring the idea as freshwater scarcity worsens
item.description: In a bold venture back in 1977, a Saudi prince attempted to tow an iceberg to address a water supply dilemma. This audacious project confronted considerable engineering hurdles and substantial expenses. With current desalination methods proving both expensive and environmentally taxing, the growing issue of iceberg melting has rekindled interest. Engineers are now revisiting the practicality of transporting icebergs as a viable source of freshwater.

item.title: Faulty Ola scooter, no proper service: Consumer panel orders Rs 1.04 lakh refund, compensation
item.description: A Kerala consumer commission found Ola Electric guilty of service deficiency and unfair trade practices. The commission ordered Ola Electric to refund the scooter's full purchase price. This decision followed repeated scooter defects and a lack of proper after-sales support. The customer experienced significant financial loss and mental stress due to these issues. Ola Electric must now pay compensation and complaint costs within thirty days.
item.dc:creator: TOI Legal Desk

item.title: Plastic found in Amazon fish as particles become trapped in river plants
item.description: Plastic pollution is alarmingly prevalent among fish in the Amazon, leading to serious complications in their gills and digestive systems. The surrounding aquatic vegetation along the river captures plastic waste, forming hazardous exposure hotspots. Certain fish species can breathe air, but this adaptation makes them more susceptible to microplastics, as their smaller gills limit their capabilities to filter out harmful pollutants.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: America poisoned prairie dogs for decades, but scientists found they sustain healthy grasslands
item.description: Prairie dogs were once viewed as pests but are now recognized as ecological assets. Their burrowing and grazing improve soil and water infiltration significantly. These small mammals help prevent grasslands from turning into shrublands. Areas with prairie dogs also provide more forage for livestock and store more carbon. The loss of prairie dogs diminishes crucial ecosystem services for both nature and people.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: In 1868, an eclipse in India revealed an element found on Earth 27 years later
item.description: During the solar eclipse of 1868 in India, astronomers stumbled upon an enigmatic yellow spectral line, initially observed by Pierre Jules Janssen. Although its significance was not immediately recognized, Norman Lockyer soon named the unidentified element helium upon further analysis. Eventually, William Ramsay verified helium's presence on Earth in 1895 by extracting it from a mineral, solidifying Janssen's pioneering approach to studying solar prominences.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Meet Red Handfish, the endangered 'walking' fish that became Photo Ark's 18,000th species
item.description: For 20 years, photographer Joel Sartore has been documenting animals through his Photo Ark project, which has now reached its 18,000th species. The latest addition is the critically endangered red handfish, a tiny marine fish that uses its fins to move across the seafloor. Sartore hopes the project will raise awareness about threatened species and help preserve a record of animals that could disappear.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Discarded salon hair is being transformed into an oil-absorbing barrier that protects mangroves from oil spills in Rio de Janeiro
item.description: Discarded human hair is now preventing oil pollution in Rio de Janeiro's Guanabara Bay. Each gram of hair absorbs approximately five grams of oil, repelling water effectively. These hair barriers, made from salon waste, can remain in the water for four months. The initiative protects vulnerable mangrove ecosystems from chronic and everyday oil leaks. This innovative project aims to aid the recovery of the bay's marine life.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: The Netherlands built new islands from 37 million tonnes of lake sediment
item.description: In an innovative move, Dutch engineers have fashioned new islands from lake sediment to rejuvenate a fragile freshwater ecosystem. These manmade structures have swiftly drawn an array of flora and fauna, notably various bird populations. The initiative has revitalised an ailing lake, transforming it into a bustling habitat for marine life and migratory birds alike.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: California’s Shasta Dam flooded Kennett, a copper-mining town beneath Lake Shasta
item.description: Once a bustling northern California mining hub, Kennett was swallowed by the depths of Shasta Lake following the construction of the Shasta Dam. This ambitious federal project aimed at water management inundated the town, which thrived on copper mining and railroads. Today, only historical accounts and the lake itself hint at the vibrant community that once existed in this submerged landscape.
